oai_dc:dc.dc:title: “They shall not pass!”: British Anti-fascists and the Politics of Violence
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: In the 1970s, British anti-fascists resorted to force to prevent the National Front from operating in public. In the 1980s and 1990s, similar tactics were used against the British National Party. This violence was politically motivated and was the latest episode in a long history of militant anti-fascism. It bore only superficial similarities with other forms of mass disorder such as football hooliganism. From 2009, British anti-fascists had to face a new adversary in the form of the English Defence League (EDL), created by extreme right-wing activists and football hooligans. Despite the provocative nature of the EDL’s activities, anti-fascists did not mount a serious campaign of violent opposition. This can be explained by the evolution of the far left, the specificities of the EDL, changes in the labour movement, as well as more repressive policing.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Online Journeying within the Pitt Rivers Cook-Voyage Collections
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Travel was one of the means by which objects were amassed and, if viewed from afar, in space and time, these artefacts may be considered as discursive repositories, other than textual, which compile narratives of journeys. Investigating the mechanics of mediation of these objects (as for text and image) may then be understood as research work in the field of Travel Studies. Artefacts in ethnographic collections have been the object of decolonizing attention and scholarship which challenge for example static, exhibitive on-site praxes. I will thus approach what I will consider as the connected triptych of Travel Studies, “cargo” and the decolonial turn within the framework of a case-study, using the online presentation of the Cook-Voyage Collection at the Pitt Rivers Museum (Oxford) (PRM) as an entry point. The focus will be on specifically digital showcasing, not of exhibitions but of catalogues of online collections /databases of ethnographic objects, which in the absence of decolonial enquiry and action, may well continue to generate elliptical, partial or fragmented experiences of virtual journeying.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: “If It Means Lives Lost That is How it Must Be”: The Ethics of Strike Action in the NHS, from the Winter of Discontent to the Nurses’ Strike of 2022-2023
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Ethical questions are seldom asked about trade union activities and of trade unionists themselves. Both scholars of labour history and industrial relations and trade unionists themselves would regard the altering of the balance of forces with the employers and the state as the key political question in relation to collective action. Still, there exists an area of trade union activism and scholarly interest where one finds a body of literature discussing the place of ethics in collective action, namely in health service unionism and in research on collective action taken by health service workers. This article first discusses the foregrounding of ethical concern as a key discursive device in anti-union, anti-strike coverage of industrial disputes in the UK National Health Service. It then looks at how the development of health service trade unionism in the 1970s was conceived, by trade unionists and scholars alike, as a move away, a liberation from ethical concern, in a mirror image of the anti-strike discourses. Finally, the article looks at the embedded ethics of strike action during the 2022-2023 UK nurses’ strike.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: George Orwell and the Spirit of Protest
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article examines George Orwell’s lifelong cultivation of what is termed the ‘spirit of protest’, a commitment to individual heterodoxy, truth‑telling, and resistance to political orthodoxy. Drawing on Orwell’s essays, fiction, diaries, and political activities, it traces his scepticism toward collective protest movements and his preference for dissent expressed through individual judgement and literary integrity. The discussion situates Orwell alongside writers such as Koestler, Zamyatin, and Camus, highlighting a shared belief in the necessity of perpetual protest against ideological conformity. The article argues that Orwell conceived protest primarily as a writerly vocation, rooted in linguistic clarity and moral honesty, and that Nineteen Eighty‑Four functions as a warning about the annihilation of this spirit through repression, surveillance, historical erasure, and manufactured conformity. Ultimately, it contends that Orwell’s work champions the preservation of heterodoxy as essential to resisting totalitarian tendencies and sustaining the possibility of a free future.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: The Periodical The Examiner’s Coverage of the Crimean War in 1854 and the Problems of the Concept of Progress
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The weekly periodical The Examiner is well-known by name to historians of Victorian Britain but no serious attempts appear ever to have been made to investigate its precise profile over its approximately eighty-year publication run or to identify exactly what justifies its habitual qualification as ‘progressive’ or ‘radical’ or whether such ‘progressivism’ or ‘radicalism’ implied different, fluctuating values as the nineteenth century wore on. Famously, the periodical was where Alfred Tennyson chose to publish his Charge of the Light Brigade, itself an ambiguous reflection on aristocratic military ‘blundering’ during the Battle of Balaclava (1854), and the Crimean War of 1853-1856 offers itself up as rich case study material revealing markers of the Examiner’s purported progressive values and their evolution over time. After establishing a reasonably solid understanding of the nature and profile of the periodical’s editorial staff, this article draws on extensive, and hitherto largely under-investigated, primary source material both from key historical moments before the Crimean War and from key moments during the siege of Sevastopol. It will be shown that the aura of revolt associated with The Examiner in its fiery inaugural years had faded by the time of the Crimean War, partly because of historical change, but also partly because of the innate ambiguities of the concept of progress and its complex relationship to bourgeois goals and ideology.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: “The Interests of All Exploited People Are the Same”: An Analysis of Orwell’s Socialist Perspective
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: George Orwell’s satires, Animal Farm (1945) and 1984 (1949), stand as two of the most iconic political satires of the twentieth century century. They offer forceful expressions of how revolutions are betrayed by the corrupting effects of power, ultimately resulting in regimes more repressive than those they replaced. Yet what began as an internal critique of Socialism was soon recast as an argument against revolution and Socialism. Since his untimely death in 1949, the Left has decried Orwell’s betrayal of its cause, while the Right has appropriated his anti-totalitarian rhetoric in its war against Communism. By situating Orwell’s political and moral thought within its historical context — the turbulent decades of the 1930s and 1940s, marked by capitalism’s deepest crisis, the rise of Fascism and Soviet Communism, and the Second World War — this article seeks to reexamine Orwell’s political thought in the context of the political crises of the first half of the twentieth century, and to reconsider his work in a new light.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: George Cruikshank (1792-1878) in Protest: The Artist as a “Public Moralist”
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: George Cruikshank (1792-1878) was a British illustrator and satirist who used not only his art as a form of protest, but also other forms of communication, such as pamphlets, letters to the press, and oration. Cruikshank’s diverse causes include political lampoons which critique government attempts to suppress this very form of protest, social reforms, and a zealous, almost dogmatic, involvement with the Temperance movement. Taking into account the diversity of the objects and forms of Cruikshank’s protest, this paper will seek to explore the ethical and ideological motivations which led him to engage in public debate, the evolution of his ideas, and his place in a wider ideological context. Examining his expressed desire to impact government or individual actions, we will argue that the many forms of his protest contribute to establish the artist as a Victorian public moralist.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: The Liberal Radicalism of T.H. Green and Edward Caird
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article gives a new perspective on the relationship between liberalism, class and protest in the late-Victorian and Edwardian political thought and activism. It focuses particularly on two leading British idealists, Thomas Hill Green (1836-82) and Edward Caird (1835-1908). Section one introduces the topic. Section two argues against a wide-spread scholarly interpretation of the British idealists as moralising middle-class collectivists. Section three argues that Green was a radical who foregrounded the experiences of the working classes in his practical activism. Section four argues much the same for Edward Caird, relying on his understudied lectures on social ethics. The article concludes that this analysis demonstrates that socially-embedded liberalism can ground a theory of radical class-sensitive politics. Throughout, the article uses a range of sources including previously obscure newspaper reports in local newspapers.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Implementation of assessments in mathematics teacher learning during the covid-19 pandemic: A case study
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The aims of this study were to: (1) provide an overview of the implementation of assessments in mathematics learning carried out by mathematics teachers at MAN 2 Bone during the covid-19 pandemic, (2) find out the obstacles and obstacles for MAN 2 Bone teachers in carrying out mathematics assessments during the pandemic. covid-19 The research method used is descriptive analysis with quantitative and qualitative approaches. Data were obtained through a questionnaire/questionnaire and interviews. The results showed that the implementation of the assessment carried out by MAN 2 Bone teachers in learning mathematics during the pandemic period was quite well implemented. Even so, there are still teachers who experience problems in carrying out math assessments during the COVID-19 pandemic, starting from the difficulty of assessing students' conceptual understanding of mathematics to the decision to determine the final grade of the semester during the COVID-19 pandemic.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Conceptualisations du genre dans les discours de savoirs linguistiques
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: In this article, I explore how various linguistic discourses conceptualise gender. By focusing on matters of reference and the extra-linguistic dimension, we can understand which sex/gender conceptions are at play in the linguistic analyses, and therefore how linguistics carries, reproduces or challenges various views on gender (such as natural or as a social order, etc.). More broadly, these analyses provide insights into how grammatical analyses conceptualise the extra-linguistic world to which language refers or that language designates.Using the notion of anti-essentialism as a benchmark, I first focus on 20th-century structuralism, then on the field of typology, and finally on the feminist linguistics from the 1990s. I also discuss some classifications of the various kinds of « genders » existing in Gender & Language Studies.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Dis/continuité référentielle dans les fabliaux médiévaux : variation de genre, points de vue et chaînes anaphoriques
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The comic effect of certain medieval fabliaux is based on the act of cross-dressing: the hero of the story, thanks to a perfectly successful disguise, manages to pass as a person of the opposite sex. However, this doubling of identity is only accessible for certain points of view. From the narrator’s perspective, male and female identities are merely two faces of a single human referent; but for other characters in the story, they are two distinct referents. This raises the issue of referential continuity: a single referent develops multiple anaphoric chains, the nature of which is determined by the point of view applied. In our article, we first analyse the structure of the anaphoric chains associated with cross-dressed referents, highlighting the constraints related to coreferential continuity. Then, we examine the predicates linked to these cross-dressed referents, paying particular attention to the isotopy conflicts induced by the act of cross-dressing. Through a detailed textual analysis of the fabliaux Trubert, Berangier au lonc Cul, and La Saineresse, we address the relationship between gender (a linguistic category), sex (a biological category), and the cultural representation of sex (isotopies).
